doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Researching finger style guitar history and chord progressions
summary: He discusses his Hal Leonard folio on the evolution of finger style guitar, from 1507 lute tablature on, and how old chord progressions persist into jazz and pop.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The Original Dixieland Jazz Band. Yeah. Notwithstanding the fact that you had many artists earlier than that. My focus has been, in fact since we were last together, my focus has been on the history of finger style guitar and the instruments. And I put out of folio last year with Hal Leonard called “The Evolution of Finger Style Guitar.” And I started with transcriptions of lute music from 1507 from Petrucci’s first folio of lute tablature, and then followed that through Baroque guitar and Renaissance guitar, Baroque guitar, classical, into the earlier twentieth century and really followed kind of the timeline and the stylistic areas and just how much — one of the things that really became evident to

me was how much the concept of the chord progression, like we experience it in jazz you know, rhythm changes or whatever, has its historical antecedents in the sixteenth century you had the Romanesque, the passa mezzo maderno — that these progressions actually still get used even today. You know the Romanesque being the kind of the foundation of the “Greensleeves” progression. And then in the baroque era the vihuela or the vihuelo d’espania progression, which the closest — the pop song that was written on that is “Green Leaves of Summer” is actually on the vihuela progression and you can find that progression from Corelli, Lully, through Beethoven in the Fifth Symphony Second Movement. Rachmaninoff, and into pop song writing. And how much these concepts of chord progressions really kind of date back to the sixteenth century where the dominant instruments were fretted string instruments like the lute and the huala in Spain and then the renaissance guitar. In the early — there were keyboards but they were still fairly rudimentary, and how that area of kind of crossover between folk music practices, popular music practices in their own era, and what became kind of musicologically defined as classical music. There’s a very gray area in between all that. What’s fascinating to me is how much improvisation was a big part of that, even through into the early nineteenth century.
